interviewQuestions.question: What problem does a service mesh solve that a gateway doesn't, and how does it solve it without changing application code?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A gateway secures and shapes north-south traffic at the edge, but has zero visibility into east-west traffic — the calls services make to each other internally. As service count grows past a handful, that internal traffic needs the same concerns applied consistently: encryption in transit, retries with backoff, timeouts, and per-hop observability. A mesh exists to give you that without every team building it themselves.

The mechanism is the sidecar pattern: a lightweight proxy, almost always Envoy, runs alongside every service instance and transparently intercepts its inbound and outbound traffic via iptables redirection (or eBPF in newer designs). The application makes a completely normal outbound HTTP or gRPC call; the OS-level redirect routes it into the local sidecar first, which applies mTLS, retries, and load-balancing before the request ever leaves the Pod. The app never imports a mesh SDK and never knows the mesh exists — that's the specific property that lets a mesh work uniformly across Go, Java, and Python services with zero code change to any of them.

A concrete payoff: rolling out mTLS across 20 services written in three different languages without touching a single line of source, because the control plane issues certificates and every sidecar enforces encryption identically regardless of what's running inside the Pod. Try to do that with a shared library instead, and you need three separate library implementations, each independently correct, each independently upgraded when the crypto library has a CVE.

The cost is real too — an extra proxy hop per call, sidecar CPU/memory per Pod, and a new control plane to operate — which is why the earlier fundamentals topic frames this as a decision gated on scale, not a default.

**Testing:** whether you see the sidecar as the mechanism that decouples cross-cutting concerns from app code, not just a buzzword for "the mesh does networking."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: What a mesh solves, and how

interviewQuestions.question: What's the difference between a mesh's data plane and control plane, and why keep them separate?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The data plane is every sidecar proxy actually handling live traffic in real time — it's on the critical path of every single request, so it has to be fast and has to keep working even under stress. The control plane (Istiod, in Istio) never touches a request at all; its job is computing routing rules, issuing and rotating certificates, and evaluating policy, then pushing the resulting configuration out to every proxy over the xDS protocol.

Separating them buys two things. First, centralized change with distributed execution: update a routing rule or rotate a cluster-wide certificate in one place, and it propagates to every proxy automatically, instead of touching N services individually — this is what makes mesh-wide mTLS rollout or a canary weight change a single API call rather than N deploys. Second, and more important operationally, it isolates blast radius: if the control plane goes briefly unreachable — a bad deploy, a network partition — every sidecar keeps proxying traffic on its last-known-good configuration. The mesh doesn't go down because Istiod did; it just stops *learning new things* until the connection recovers. A mesh where the data plane froze the instant the control plane was unreachable would make Istiod a single point of failure for all production traffic, which defeats the purpose.

This is the same shape as Kubernetes' own split — the control plane (API server, scheduler, controller-manager) decides desired state, kubelets on each node execute it and keep workloads running even through a brief control-plane outage. Recognizing this as a recurring pattern, not something unique to meshes, is usually the signal an interviewer is checking for.

**Testing:** whether you see the split as a deliberate, load-bearing separation of concerns, and can connect it to the same pattern elsewhere in infrastructure.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why separate the two planes

interviewQuestions.question: A junior engineer suggests replacing the mesh with a shared retry/timeout library imported by every service — wouldn't that be simpler? How would you respond?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It would be simpler for a while, and I'd say so honestly rather than dismissing the idea — a shared library is a completely reasonable choice at small scale, and it's exactly what I'd recommend for a handful of services in one language. The mesh isn't universally better; it trades one set of costs for another, and which trade wins depends on scale and language diversity.

Where the library breaks down: it only works if every service is in a language that library supports, and it only stays correct if every service actually upgrades to the new version when the retry logic gets a bug fix — in practice, with enough teams, some services run six-month-old versions of the library with a known-bad backoff algorithm, because upgrading a dependency isn't anyone's top priority until it causes an incident. A mesh sidesteps both problems: it works identically regardless of the app's language, and a policy change takes effect for every service the moment the control plane pushes it, with no per-service deploy or dependency bump required.

The second gap: a shared library can't do anything that requires visibility *across* the call, like mTLS between two services or consistent distributed tracing headers — those need something sitting outside the process, observing every hop the same way, which is structurally what a sidecar is and a library isn't.

So my answer to the junior engineer would be: name the actual trigger for the mesh — polyglot services, or org size where a library rollout genuinely can't happen atomically — rather than either dismissing the suggestion or agreeing to a mesh by default. If those triggers aren't present yet, their instinct might be right.

**Testing:** whether you can validate a simpler alternative on its merits instead of defending the mesh as always correct.
